body: Oil Traders Want U.S. to Release Sanctioned Tankers as Freight Costs Soar What I Cover Irina Slav has been writing about global energy markets since 2007, covering the oil and gas industry, energy security, commodities, and the… The wars in Ukraine and the Middle East have prompted an increase in EV sales to avoid retail fuel inflation and gas demand destruction in favor of other power generation sources. With COP31 starting next week, some participants have signaled that faster electrification could become the focus of the event. “I would like to see a strong outcome on electrification in our presidency-led decision,” this year’s COP’s head of negotiations, Australian climate change minister Chris Bowen, told Bloomberg. Bowen also said he would consider COP31 a success if all participating countries made a commitment to increase the share of electricity in their final energy demand mix. Final energy is the kind that is actually used, as opposed to primary energy, which is energy in its raw form. While crude oil, for instance, is primary energy, gasoline, diesel, and jet fuel are final energy. Electricity is also a form of final energy, with its primary input coming from primary coal, gas, water, geothermal, and, more recently, solar and wind energy. It is those two latter sources of energy that COP leaders have selected as favorites for the grid of the near and far future—but have so far failed to make dominant. The world still sources over 80% of its primary energy from hydrocarbons. In other words, over 80% of the energy resources that the world consumes come from oil, gas, and coal. But, according to Bloomberg’s Zero podcast host, Akshat Rathi, by the time the energy goes from primary to final, the share of hydrocarbons falls to 65%. “Thus electrification is foremost an energy efficiency solution, because it reduces primary energy demand without cutting the useful outcomes that citizens want,” Rathi wrote in a recent report on COP31 ambitions. Electrification is the ultimate goal of the energy transition in every industry and aspect of life, excluding, perhaps chemicals production and related fields that rely on hydrocarbon feedstock for their output. Yet it is not just any electrification, of course, that transition advocates promote. Electrification must come from wind, solar, biomass, geothermal, hydro, and nuclear if it is to be done the right way, in view of emission reduction targets agreed a decade ago in Paris. Related: The Iran War Isn't Over, but Oil Traders Are Already Pricing In Peace Over these past ten years, trillions have been invested in the goal of electrification. Indeed, transition investment just last year hit $2.3 trillion, according to BloombergNEF . This was 8% higher than total transition investment during the previous year—and there was not even a war in the Middle East to cause the most serious disruption to oil and gas supply in history. The biggest portion of that total went into transport electrification, and the second-biggest portion went into wind and solar capacity. The buildout in electric vehicles, wind, and solar generation capacity and related technologies over the past 10 years has been quite impressive. It has failed to reduce global emissions of carbon dioxide, but it has led to regional declines, for instance in Europe, by means of energy demand destruction, mostly by discouragement through higher costs resulting from emission reduction policies.
